items.stem: Define the term 'data'.
items.answer: Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, characters or symbols, that have no context and so no meaning on their own.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, characters or symbols, that have no context and so no meaning on their own. [2]

items.stem: Explain why "35, 42, 38" is data and not information.
items.answer: The values have no context: we do not know what they measure or what units they are in, so they have no meaning.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: no context/meaning; 1 mark: e.g. we do not know if they are ages, marks or temperatures. [2]

items.stem: Explain two advantages of using a direct data source.
items.answer: The exact data needed is collected, so there is no irrelevant data; the source and collection method are known so the data can be trusted; it is up to date.
items.markingKey: 2 × 1 mark point + 1 mark explanation, from: only relevant data; known reliability/origin; up to date; can be sampled appropriately. [4]

items.stem: Arjun works for GreenLeaf Pharmacy, a pharmacy in Cairo. Arjun needs data to decide whether to open on Sundays. Explain one advantage of using a direct data source rather than an indirect one in this situation.
items.answer: Only relevant data is collected and it is up to date, so decisions are based on current, appropriate data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation in context. [2]

items.stem: The manager of Northfield Academy in Nairobi wants to know how satisfied customers are with its online service. (a) Explain one disadvantage of using indirect data in this situation. (b) Give an example of a piece of data that might be collected and explain how it becomes information.
items.answer: (a) It may be out of date or collected for a different purpose, so it may not reflect current customers or this area. (b) e.g. "45" becomes information when it is given context: "45% of customers would shop on Sundays".
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark explanation in context. [2] (b) 1 mark example of data; 1 mark context/processing added. [2]

items.stem: SkyLink Airways, an airline based in Seoul, is planning a new branch in a nearby district and needs data about the people who live there. Discuss whether SkyLink Airways should rely on indirect data sources rather than collecting its own data.
items.answer: Points for: indirect data is quicker and cheaper; large datasets; available immediately. Points against / limitations: may be out of date; collected for another purpose so may not fit; unknown accuracy or bias; may have to be bought. Conclusion: a combination is often best: use indirect data for an overview and direct data for the specific decision.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: indirect data is quicker and cheaper; large datasets; available immediately. Against: may be out of date; collected for another purpose so may not fit; unknown accuracy or bias; may have to be bought. Conclusion may argue: a combination is often best: use indirect data for an overview and direct data for the specific decision. [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'direct data source' and 'knowledge'.
items.answer: direct data source: Data that is collected first-hand by the person or organisation that will use it, for the specific purpose it is needed for. knowledge: Information that has been understood and combined with experience so that it can be applied, for example to make decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direct data source correctly described; 1 mark: knowledge correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem:
For each situation, state whether the data source is direct or indirect and give a reason for each.
1. A teacher observes pupils in a lesson and notes how often they ask questions.
2. A travel company buys a list of email addresses from a marketing firm.
3. An estate agent uses house prices published on a property website.
items.answer: 1 direct; 2 indirect; 3 indirect
items.markingKey: 1: direct (first-hand, for this purpose); 2: indirect (second-hand / collected for another purpose); 3: indirect (second-hand / collected for another purpose) — 1 mark each classification, 1 mark each reason. [6]

items.stem: Leila, a researcher at Orbit Games Studio in Seoul, is investigating how local people travel to work and to the shops. Discuss whether Orbit Games Studio should rely on indirect data sources rather than collecting its own data.
items.answer: Points for: indirect data is quicker and cheaper; large datasets; available immediately. Points against / limitations: may be out of date; collected for another purpose so may not fit; unknown accuracy or bias; may have to be bought. Conclusion: a combination is often best: use indirect data for an overview and direct data for the specific decision.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: indirect data is quicker and cheaper; large datasets; available immediately. Against: may be out of date; collected for another purpose so may not fit; unknown accuracy or bias; may have to be bought. Conclusion may argue: a combination is often best: use indirect data for an overview and direct data for the specific decision. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'accuracy (of information)'.
items.answer: Information is accurate when it is correct and free from errors, so it can be relied on.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Information is accurate when it is correct and free from errors, so it can be relied on. [2]

items.stem: Explain why information that is accurate may still be of poor quality.
items.answer: It may be out of date, irrelevant to the purpose, incomplete or have the wrong level of detail, so it still cannot be used to make a good decision.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: accuracy is only one factor; 1 mark: example of another factor making it unusable. [2]

items.stem: Explain how the age of information can affect the decisions made by a business.
items.answer: Old information may no longer reflect the current situation (e.g. prices, stock levels, customer numbers), so decisions such as how much to order may be wrong.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: out of date no longer reflects reality; 1 mark: consequence for a decision. [2]

items.stem: The managers of FreshFarm Foods in Dhaka complain that the information they receive is not helping them make decisions. Explain why the information must be up to date.
items.answer: Decisions are based on the current situation; old information (e.g. prices, timetables, stock levels) may have changed, leading to wrong decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: changes over time; 1 mark: consequence. [2]

items.stem: Isla is using information from several websites to plan a business trip from Manila to Muscat. (a) Explain why the information must be up to date. (b) Explain why the information needs to be complete.
items.answer: (a) Decisions are based on the current situation; old information (e.g. prices, timetables, stock levels) may have changed, leading to wrong decisions. (b) If parts are missing, the user cannot make a full judgement and may have to search for more information or make mistakes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: changes over time; 1 mark: consequence. [2] (b) 1 mark: missing parts; 1 mark: consequence. [2]

items.stem: Lucas is using information from several websites to plan a business trip from Toronto to Bangkok. Evaluate how far the quality of the information affects the decisions made by Orbit Games Studio.
items.answer: Points for: accurate, relevant, current and complete information leads to better decisions and fewer costly mistakes. Points against / limitations: managers' experience (knowledge) also matters; sometimes decisions must be made quickly with imperfect information; collecting perfect information is expensive. Conclusion: quality is critical, but the cost of improving it must be balanced against the benefit to the decision.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: accurate, relevant, current and complete information leads to better decisions and fewer costly mistakes. Against: managers' experience (knowledge) also matters; sometimes decisions must be made quickly with imperfect information; collecting perfect information is expensive. Conclusion may argue: quality is critical, but the cost of improving it must be balanced against the benefit to the decision. [4]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'accuracy (of information)' and 'level of detail'.
items.answer: accuracy (of information): Information is accurate when it is correct and free from errors, so it can be relied on. level of detail: Whether information contains the right amount of detail for its purpose: not too much and not too little.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: accuracy (of information) correctly described; 1 mark: level of detail correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: The managers of Lakeside College in Mexico City complain that the information they receive is not helping them make decisions. (a) Explain why the information must be up to date. (b) Describe two ways the accuracy of the data could be improved.
items.answer: (a) Decisions are based on the current situation; old information (e.g. prices, timetables, stock levels) may have changed, leading to wrong decisions. (b) Validation checks on input (range, presence, format); verification such as double entry or visual checking; using reliable sources.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: changes over time; 1 mark: consequence. [2] (b) 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Nova Telecom, a telecommunications company in Doha, produces a weekly report for managers using data entered by staff. Discuss how far the quality of the information affects the decisions made by Nova Telecom.
items.answer: Points for: accurate, relevant, current and complete information leads to better decisions and fewer costly mistakes. Points against / limitations: managers' experience (knowledge) also matters; sometimes decisions must be made quickly with imperfect information; collecting perfect information is expensive. Conclusion: quality is critical, but the cost of improving it must be balanced against the benefit to the decision.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: accurate, relevant, current and complete information leads to better decisions and fewer costly mistakes. Against: managers' experience (knowledge) also matters; sometimes decisions must be made quickly with imperfect information; collecting perfect information is expensive. Conclusion may argue: quality is critical, but the cost of improving it must be balanced against the benefit to the decision. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'validation'.
items.answer: An automatic check carried out by the computer to make sure that data entered is reasonable and follows set rules.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: An automatic check carried out by the computer to make sure that data entered is reasonable and follows set rules. [2]

items.stem: Explain why data that passes validation may still be incorrect.
items.answer: Validation only checks that data is reasonable and follows the rules; a wrong value that is still within the rules (e.g. age 31 typed instead of 13) will be accepted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: validation checks reasonableness/rules only; 1 mark: suitable example. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between validation and verification.
items.answer: Validation is an automatic check that data is sensible/obeys rules; verification checks that data has been entered or copied accurately from the source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark validation; 1 mark verification. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Eagles Sports Club in Auckland type details from paper application forms into a database. Describe how double data entry would be carried out.
items.answer: Data is typed in twice, possibly by different people; the computer compares the two entries and flags any differences to be corrected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark entered twice; 1 mark compared/differences flagged. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Nova Telecom in Manila type details from paper application forms into a database. (a) Explain why verification is also needed. (b) Describe how double data entry would be carried out.
items.answer: (a) Data could pass validation but still be entered incorrectly; verification checks it matches the source. (b) Data is typed in twice, possibly by different people; the computer compares the two entries and flags any differences to be corrected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark valid but wrong data; 1 mark verification compares with source. [2] (b) 1 mark entered twice; 1 mark compared/differences flagged. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Coral Bay Aquarium in Lima type details from paper application forms into a database. (a) Describe two validation checks that could be used on the form, naming a field for each. (b) Describe how double data entry would be carried out.
items.answer: (a) e.g. presence check on surname; range check on age 16–100; format check on postcode; length check on phone number; lookup check on country. (b) Data is typed in twice, possibly by different people; the computer compares the two entries and flags any differences to be corrected.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per check with suitable field, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark entered twice; 1 mark compared/differences flagged. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Horizon Travel in Accra type details from paper application forms into a database. Discuss whether validation and verification together can guarantee that the data stored by Horizon Travel is accurate.
items.answer: Points for: validation removes unreasonable data; verification detects transcription errors; together they catch most input errors. Points against / limitations: valid but wrong data that matches a wrong source document will still be accepted; human verification can be careless; data can become out of date. Conclusion: they greatly reduce, but cannot eliminate, inaccurate data; good source data and staff training are also needed.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: validation removes unreasonable data; verification detects transcription errors; together they catch most input errors. Against: valid but wrong data that matches a wrong source document will still be accepted; human verification can be careless; data can become out of date. Conclusion may argue: they greatly reduce, but cannot eliminate, inaccurate data; good source data and staff training are also needed. [4]

items.stem: Sunrise Bakery, a bakery in Dubai, uses an online form for customers to register and place orders. Evaluate whether validation and verification together can guarantee that the data stored by Sunrise Bakery is accurate.
items.answer: Points for: validation removes unreasonable data; verification detects transcription errors; together they catch most input errors. Points against / limitations: valid but wrong data that matches a wrong source document will still be accepted; human verification can be careless; data can become out of date. Conclusion: they greatly reduce, but cannot eliminate, inaccurate data; good source data and staff training are also needed.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: validation removes unreasonable data; verification detects transcription errors; together they catch most input errors. Against: valid but wrong data that matches a wrong source document will still be accepted; human verification can be careless; data can become out of date. Conclusion may argue: they greatly reduce, but cannot eliminate, inaccurate data; good source data and staff training are also needed. [4]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'verification'.
items.answer: A check that data has been copied or entered accurately, i.e. that it matches the original source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A check that data has been copied or entered accurately, i.e. that it matches the original source. [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'check digit'.
items.answer: An extra digit added to the end of a code, calculated from the other digits, which is recalculated on input to detect errors such as transposed digits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: An extra digit added to the end of a code, calculated from the other digits, which is recalculated on input to detect errors such as transposed digits. [2]

items.stem: Lina is designing a data entry screen for the membership system of TransGlobal Logistics in Colombo. Explain why a visual check may not detect all errors.
items.answer: The person checking may be tired or careless, may misread the source, or may read what they expect to see.
items.markingKey: 1 mark human error; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: A library uses a modulo-11 check digit on its book codes. Each digit is multiplied by a weight, starting at 5 for the leftmost digit and going down to 2; the products are added; the check digit is (11 − (total MOD 11)) MOD 11, with 10 written as X. Calculate the check digit for the code 7373. Show your working.
Define the term 'batch processing'.
items.answer: Processing in which data is collected together over a period of time and then processed all at once, without user interaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Processing in which data is collected together over a period of time and then processed all at once, without user interaction. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a transaction file is sorted before it is used to update a sequential master file.
items.answer: Both files are then in the same key order, so the master file can be read once from start to end, matching each transaction to its record; this is efficient and needs no searching.
items.markingKey: 1 mark same key order; 1 mark read sequentially once / efficient. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a new master file is created during a batch update rather than changing the old one.
items.answer: Records cannot easily be changed in place in a sequential file; writing a new file also keeps the old master and the transaction file as a backup (grandfather–father–son) if the update fails.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sequential update writes new file; 1 mark old file kept as backup/recovery. [2]

items.stem: Starlight Cinemas, a cinema chain in Dubai, keeps customer records on a master file that is updated from a transaction file every night. Explain why batch processing is suitable here.
items.answer: Large volumes of similar data can be collected over a period and processed together, at off-peak times, without user interaction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark large volume/collected first; 1 mark no interaction/off-peak. [2]

items.stem: Jonas manages the IT systems at Lotus Fashion in Mexico City, which handles both online bookings and a monthly payroll. (a) Explain why batch processing is suitable here. (b) Explain why the old master file is kept after the update.
items.answer: (a) Large volumes of similar data can be collected over a period and processed together, at off-peak times, without user interaction. (b) If the new master is lost or corrupted, it can be recreated by running the old master with the transaction file again (backup / recovery).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark large volume/collected first; 1 mark no interaction/off-peak. [2] (b) 1 mark backup; 1 mark recreated from old master + transactions. [2]

items.stem: Hana manages the IT systems at Vista Estate Agents in Madrid, which handles both online bookings and a monthly payroll. (a) Describe what is stored on the master file and on the transaction file. (b) Explain why the old master file is kept after the update.
items.answer: (a) Master file: permanent data such as customer ID, name, address and balance. Transaction file: changes over the period, such as payments, new orders or meter readings. (b) If the new master is lost or corrupted, it can be recreated by running the old master with the transaction file again (backup / recovery).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark master; 1 mark transaction. [2] (b) 1 mark backup; 1 mark recreated from old master + transactions. [2]

items.stem: SwiftCar Rentals, a car rental company in Accra, collects data about its customers during each month and sends out invoices in one run. Evaluate whether SwiftCar Rentals should replace its overnight batch processing with online processing.
items.answer: Points for: files always up to date; customers see current information; errors found immediately. Points against / limitations: more expensive hardware and continuous availability needed; heavier load at peak times; batch is efficient for large regular jobs such as bills. Conclusion: a mixed approach is usual: online for transactions customers see, batch for large periodic jobs.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: files always up to date; customers see current information; errors found immediately. Against: more expensive hardware and continuous availability needed; heavier load at peak times; batch is efficient for large regular jobs such as bills. Conclusion may argue: a mixed approach is usual: online for transactions customers see, batch for large periodic jobs. [4]

items.stem: Priya manages the IT systems at Delta Water Utility in Hanoi, which handles both online bookings and a monthly payroll. Evaluate whether Delta Water Utility should replace its overnight batch processing with online processing.
items.answer: Points for: files always up to date; customers see current information; errors found immediately. Points against / limitations: more expensive hardware and continuous availability needed; heavier load at peak times; batch is efficient for large regular jobs such as bills. Conclusion: a mixed approach is usual: online for transactions customers see, batch for large periodic jobs.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: files always up to date; customers see current information; errors found immediately. Against: more expensive hardware and continuous availability needed; heavier load at peak times; batch is efficient for large regular jobs such as bills. Conclusion may argue: a mixed approach is usual: online for transactions customers see, batch for large periodic jobs. [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'transaction file' and 'online processing'.
items.answer: transaction file: A temporary file holding the changes (transactions) collected over a period, which are used to update the master file. online processing: Processing in which each transaction is processed as soon as it is entered, while the user interacts with the system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: transaction file correctly described; 1 mark: online processing correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of batch processing.
items.answer: Advantage: can run at off-peak times (e.g. overnight) with no staff present, processing large volumes efficiently. Disadvantage: the master file is out of date between runs, and errors are found only after the run.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage + explanation; 1 mark disadvantage + explanation. [4]

items.stem: Which type of processing is most suitable for a heart-rate monitor that sounds an alarm in an intensive care unit?
items.answer: Real-time processing
items.markingKey: Real-time: readings must be processed immediately so an alarm can sound without delay.

items.stem:
State the most suitable type of processing (batch, online or real-time) for each task and justify your choice.
1. Producing the monthly payroll for 3000 employees.
2. A heart-rate monitor that sounds an alarm in an intensive care unit.
3. Controlling the temperature of a chemical reactor.
items.answer: 1: batch — all the data can be collected first and processed together without user interaction; no immediate output needed; 2: real-time — readings must be processed immediately so an alarm can sound without delay; 3: real-time — immediate response to sensor readings is needed to keep the process safe
items.markingKey: 1: batch [1], justification: all the data can be collected first and processed together without user interaction; no immediate output needed [1]; 2: real-time [1], justification: readings must be processed immediately so an alarm can sound without delay [1]; 3: real-time [1], justification: immediate response to sensor readings is needed to keep the process safe [1]. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'encryption'.
items.answer: Scrambling data (plaintext) using an algorithm and a key into a form (ciphertext) that cannot be understood without the key to decrypt it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Scrambling data (plaintext) using an algorithm and a key into a form (ciphertext) that cannot be understood without the key to decrypt it. [2]

items.stem: Explain why encryption does not stop data from being intercepted.
items.answer: Encryption does not prevent data being copied or intercepted; it makes intercepted data meaningless without the decryption key.
items.markingKey: 1 mark data can still be intercepted; 1 mark cannot be understood without key. [2]

items.stem: Explain why asymmetric encryption solves the key distribution problem of symmetric encryption.
items.answer: The public key can be shared openly because it can only encrypt; only the private key, which is never sent, can decrypt, so no secret key needs to be transmitted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark public key shared openly; 1 mark private key never transmitted/only it decrypts. [2]

items.stem: Sipho works from home and connects to the file server of Meridian Hospital in Auckland over the internet. Explain one drawback of symmetric encryption in this situation.
items.answer: Both parties need the same secret key, which must be shared securely; if it is intercepted, all messages can be decrypted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark key must be shared; 1 mark risk if intercepted. [2]

items.stem: Kwame works from home and connects to the file server of Palm Grove Hotel in Dhaka over the internet. (a) Describe how asymmetric encryption would be used to send the data securely. (b) Describe the purpose of a digital certificate.
items.answer: (a) The sender obtains the receiver's public key and uses it to encrypt the data; only the receiver's private key can decrypt it. (b) It authenticates the server by linking its identity to its public key, signed by a trusted certificate authority.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark public key of receiver encrypts; 1 mark private key decrypts. [2] (b) 1 mark authentication/identity; 1 mark issued/signed by CA. [2]

items.stem: Staff at Coral Bay Aquarium in Istanbul email confidential reports to a partner company in Doha. Evaluate whether using HTTPS is enough to protect the personal data of the customers of Coral Bay Aquarium.
items.answer: Points for: TLS encrypts data in transit and authenticates the server; protects card details from interception. Points against / limitations: data stored on the server is not protected by HTTPS; phishing sites can also have certificates; weak passwords and malware remain threats. Conclusion: HTTPS is essential but must be combined with encryption at rest, access control and staff training.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: TLS encrypts data in transit and authenticates the server; protects card details from interception. Against: data stored on the server is not protected by HTTPS; phishing sites can also have certificates; weak passwords and malware remain threats. Conclusion may argue: HTTPS is essential but must be combined with encryption at rest, access control and staff training. [4]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'symmetric encryption'.
items.answer: Encryption in which the same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Encryption in which the same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data. [2]

items.stem: Describe how a digital certificate helps a browser to trust a website.
items.answer: The certificate is issued by a trusted certificate authority and contains the website's public key and identity; the browser checks the CA's digital signature and the dates, so it knows the public key really belongs to that site.
items.markingKey: 1 mark issued by CA; 1 mark contains public key/identity; 1 mark browser verifies signature/validity. [3]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'information'.
items.answer: Data that has been processed and given context, so that it has meaning and is useful.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Data that has been processed and given context, so that it has meaning and is useful. [2]

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of using an indirect data source.
items.answer: The data may be out of date because it was collected earlier; it may contain data that is not needed or be missing data that is needed; the original collection method and possible bias are unknown.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation): out of date; irrelevant/extra data; missing data; unknown accuracy or bias; may need to be paid for. [4]

items.stem:
For each situation, state whether the data source is direct or indirect.
1. A factory manager reads the output of a sensor counting items on a conveyor belt.
2. A journalist interviews residents about a new bus route.
items.answer: 1 direct; 2 direct
items.markingKey: 1: direct (first-hand, for this purpose); 2: direct (first-hand, for this purpose) — 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: SkyLink Airways, an airline based in Accra, is planning a new branch in a nearby district and needs data about the people who live there. (a) Identify two indirect data sources that could be used. (b) Explain one disadvantage of using indirect data in this situation. (c) Describe how the information obtained could be turned into knowledge.
items.answer: (a) Government census data; published reports or statistics; the electoral register; data bought from a marketing company; other organisations' surveys. (b) It may be out of date or collected for a different purpose, so it may not reflect current customers or this area. (c) The manager interprets the information using experience, e.g. understanding that demand is high enough to cover staff costs, and uses it to make a decision.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark disadvantage; 1 mark explanation in context. [2] (c) 1 mark interpretation/understanding; 1 mark applied to a decision. [2]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'relevance (of information)'.
items.answer: Information is relevant when it relates to, and is needed for, the purpose for which it is being used.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Information is relevant when it relates to, and is needed for, the purpose for which it is being used. [2]

items.stem: Explain why too much detail can reduce the quality of information.
items.answer: The user has to search through unnecessary data to find what they need, which wastes time and the key points may be missed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: unnecessary data obscures the key points; 1 mark: time wasted / errors in decisions. [2]

items.stem: A satellite navigation system uses a map that does not show a road opened last year. Identify which factor affecting the quality of information is the main problem here and explain your answer.
items.answer: Age: the information is out of date, so it no longer reflects the current situation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: age; 1 mark: explanation — the information is out of date, so it no longer reflects the current situation. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'hash total'.
items.answer: A total of a field that has no meaning on its own, such as account numbers, used to check that all data in a batch has been entered correctly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A total of a field that has no meaning on its own, such as account numbers, used to check that all data in a batch has been entered correctly. [2]

items.stem: Explain why both validation and verification are used when entering data.
items.answer: Validation stops unreasonable data but cannot detect a valid but wrong value; verification detects transcription errors but cannot tell whether the original data was sensible; together they reduce errors more.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: what validation cannot do; 1 mark: what verification cannot do; 1 mark: combined effect. [3]

items.stem:
A clerk at Delta Water Utility prepares a batch of payment slips for input.
Account number | Amount ($)
55546 | 667.41
99127 | 43.14
83187 | 734.68
40098 | 759.96
Calculate (a) the hash total of the account numbers and (b) the control total of the amounts.

A batch of payment slips is input at Pioneer Insurance.
Account number | Amount ($)
77567 | 456.81
18306 | 650.96
23085 | 403.97
58461 | 113.21
25232 | 344.79
After input, the computer calculates a hash total of 198151 and a control total of 1,969.74. (a) Calculate the hash total of the batch. (b) Explain what the result shows.

items.stem: Yusuf is designing a data entry screen for the membership system of Atlas Museum in Cape Town. (a) Describe how double data entry would be carried out. (b) Explain why a visual check may not detect all errors.
items.answer: (a) Data is typed in twice, possibly by different people; the computer compares the two entries and flags any differences to be corrected. (b) The person checking may be tired or careless, may misread the source, or may read what they expect to see.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark entered twice; 1 mark compared/differences flagged. [2] (b) 1 mark human error; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'transaction file' and 'real-time processing'.
items.answer: transaction file: A temporary file holding the changes (transactions) collected over a period, which are used to update the master file. real-time processing: Processing in which input data is processed immediately and the output is fast enough to affect the next input, as in control systems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: transaction file correctly described; 1 mark: real-time processing correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between online processing and real-time processing.
items.answer: Online processing handles each transaction as it is entered, with the user waiting for a response; real-time processing responds immediately to inputs (often from sensors) so that the output affects the next input, as in a control system.
items.markingKey: 1 mark online; 1 mark real-time with feedback/immediate output. [2]

items.stem: Lotus Fashion, a clothing retailer in Cairo, collects data about its customers during each month and sends out invoices in one run. (a) Describe what is stored on the master file and on the transaction file. (b) Explain why batch processing is suitable here.
items.answer: (a) Master file: permanent data such as customer ID, name, address and balance. Transaction file: changes over the period, such as payments, new orders or meter readings. (b) Large volumes of similar data can be collected over a period and processed together, at off-peak times, without user interaction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark master; 1 mark transaction. [2] (b) 1 mark large volume/collected first; 1 mark no interaction/off-peak. [2]

items.stem: Freya manages the IT systems at Riverside Medical Centre in Jakarta, which handles both online bookings and a monthly payroll. (a) Describe what is stored on the master file and on the transaction file. (b) Describe the steps in updating the master file using a sorted transaction file.
items.answer: (a) Master file: permanent data such as customer ID, name, address and balance. Transaction file: changes over the period, such as payments, new orders or meter readings. (b) Read first master and first transaction; if keys match, apply the transaction and write the updated record to the new master; if master key is smaller, copy the master record unchanged; repeat until end of files; unmatched transactions written to an error report.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark master; 1 mark transaction. [2] (b) 1 mark per step, max 4. [4]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'asymmetric encryption' and 'symmetric encryption'.
items.answer: asymmetric encryption: Encryption that uses a pair of keys: a public key to encrypt data and the matching private key, kept secret by its owner, to decrypt it. symmetric encryption: Encryption in which the same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: asymmetric encryption correctly described; 1 mark: symmetric encryption correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: A Caesar cipher with key 8 shifts each letter 8 places forward in the alphabet, wrapping from Z to A. Encrypt the word SERVER.
items.answer: AMZDMZ

items.answer: SERVER. The same key (8) is used to encrypt (shift forward) and decrypt (shift back).
items.markingKey: Decryption SERVER [2] (1 mark if one error); same key used for both [1]. [3]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'knowledge'.
items.answer: Information that has been understood and combined with experience so that it can be applied, for example to make decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Information that has been understood and combined with experience so that it can be applied, for example to make decisions. [2]

items.stem: The manager of Peak Fitness in Riyadh wants to introduce using published government statistics to plan its services. Explain two drawbacks of this for the organisation.
items.answer: The data may be several years old. It may not be about the exact area or group needed.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark explanation). Advantages: data is available immediately; cheaper than collecting its own data; large sample sizes covering the whole country. items.stem: The manager of Summit Engineering in Riyadh wants to know how satisfied customers are with its online service. Identify two indirect data sources that could be used.
items.answer: Government census data; published reports or statistics; the electoral register; data bought from a marketing company; other organisations' surveys.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Noah, a researcher at City Central Library in Muscat, is investigating how local people travel to work and to the shops. Discuss the use of direct data collection methods by City Central Library when making decisions.
items.answer: Points for: relevant, current data; known reliability; can target the right people. Points against / limitations: time-consuming and costly; sample may be small or biased; respondents may not answer honestly. Conclusion: direct data is better for specific, important decisions if time and budget allow.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'age (of information)'.
items.answer: How up to date information is; out-of-date information may no longer reflect the current situation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: How up to date information is; out-of-date information may no longer reflect the current situation. [2]

items.stem: Explain how inaccurate data entry leads to inaccurate information.
items.answer: Information is produced by processing data; if the input data is wrong, the processed output will also be wrong (garbage in, garbage out).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: information depends on input data; 1 mark: GIGO consequence. [2]

items.stem: Lotus Fashion, a clothing retailer in Bangkok, produces a weekly report for managers using data entered by staff. Explain why the information must be up to date.
items.answer: Decisions are based on the current situation; old information (e.g. prices, timetables, stock levels) may have changed, leading to wrong decisions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: changes over time; 1 mark: consequence. [2]

items.stem: State what is meant by 'control total'.
items.answer: A meaningful total, such as the total value of invoices in a batch, calculated before and after input to check the data has been entered correctly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A meaningful total, such as the total value of invoices in a batch, calculated before and after input to check the data has been entered correctly. [2]

items.stem: Explain how a hash total is used to check that a batch of documents has been input correctly.
items.answer: Before input, the values of a field such as account number are added up; the computer adds the same field after input; if the totals differ, a document has been missed or mistyped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark total calculated before input; 1 mark recalculated by computer; 1 mark compared/difference shows error. [3]

items.stem: Tariq manages the IT systems at Coral Bay Aquarium in Lisbon, which handles both online bookings and a monthly payroll. Evaluate whether Coral Bay Aquarium should replace its overnight batch processing with online processing.
items.answer: Points for: files always up to date; customers see current information; errors found immediately. Points against / limitations: more expensive hardware and continuous availability needed; heavier load at peak times; batch is efficient for large regular jobs such as bills. Conclusion: a mixed approach is usual: online for transactions customers see, batch for large periodic jobs.
